slides.text: With the arrival of Gandhi, the movement for national independence reached every village, street-by-street, in Chhattisgarh. The Non-Cooperation Movement transformed lawyers into Satyagrahis and titles into surrendered medals.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: A charkha spinning in a lamplit room, its thread catching the light. The thread becoming a tricolor. Outside the window: Chhattisgarh's villages awakening. Series 1 finale. Ink-wash, warm gold tones, the quiet power of sustained resistance.

slides.text: December 26, 1920. The Nagpur Congress session. The Non-Cooperation resolution passes. Five hundred delegates from Dhamtari are in the hall, their hands raised among thousands. Chhattisgarh voted for this — not as spectators, but as participants.
slides.visualDescription: The Nagpur Congress session — a vast hall, thousands of delegates. 500 from Dhamtari visible in their section, hands raised as the Non-Cooperation resolution passes. The resolution as text on screen. History being formally voted into existence.

slides.text: Vamanrao Lakhe surrendered his Rai Sahab title — the very day the Nagpur Congress announced Non-Cooperation. The people of Raipur immediately gave him the title of Popular. The people's title replacing the empire's medal.
slides.visualDescription: Vamanrao Lakhe placing his Rai Sahab medal on a British officer's desk — walking out with nothing. Then: the crowd of Raipur garlanding him with the word Popular. Two titles: one surrendered, one received. The exchange of allegiances made visible.

slides.text: Thakur Pyarelal Singh and Ramdayal Tiwari left the practice of law. Barrister Thakkar boycotted the assembly elections he was standing for. The men closest to Gandhi's visit paid the highest personal prices — and paid them without hesitation.
slides.visualDescription: Pyarelal Singh and Tiwari hanging up their barrister robes for the last time. Barrister Thakkar withdrawing his election papers. Three men closing the professional doors that took years to open. Sacrifice as the most personal form of commitment.

slides.text: National schools opened across Chhattisgarh — Madhav Rao Sapre in Raipur, Chhotelal Srivastava in Dhamtari, Badrinath Saw in Bilaspur. Refusing British schools, building Indian ones. Education as an act of non-cooperation.
slides.visualDescription: Three national schools opening simultaneously across Chhattisgarh — children streaming through new gates. Teachers unafraid. Parents proud. The British school system being refused. Knowledge as resistance. The classroom as a front line.

slides.text: Prabhu Lal Kabra and Ratnakar Jha led a huge procession to boycott foreign goods on August 1, 1921. The boycott spreading from platform and podium to the streets, to the market, to the daily choices of ordinary people.
slides.visualDescription: August 1, 1921 — Kabra and Jha leading a procession through Raipur. Long line of people in khadi, foreign cloth burning in a pile at the market. The Non-Cooperation Movement as daily practice, not just political declaration. The street as the movement's ground.

slides.text: Mohammad Yunus stood before the British magistrate and said: 'I am involved in Mahatma Gandhi's non-cooperation movement from now on.' He walked from the courtroom to the jail. His seventeen-village zamindari, hundreds of acres, cattle, and gold — all confiscated.
slides.visualDescription: Mohammad Yunus before the magistrate — his declaration ringing out in the courtroom. Then: walking directly to jail. His zamindari — seventeen villages, vast land, cattle, gold — disappearing into British confiscation behind him. He does not look back.

slides.text: January 1922. The Nagari-Sihawa Jungle Satyagraha. Tribals entered the reserved forest in protest of the Forest Act — which banned them from their own ancestral forest. Thirty-nine were arrested. Not one apologised to the British.
slides.visualDescription: January 1922. Tribal Satyagrahis entering the reserved forest deliberately, peacefully, in organised groups. British forest officers arresting them one by one. 39 people taken. Each one standing straight. Not one bowing. The forest as the site of conscience.

slides.text: The Jungle Satyagrahis were sentenced to 3 to 5 months imprisonment. But the forest department conceded: minimum wages for forest workers were established, forced labour stopped. Small victories, won through organised dignity.
slides.visualDescription: The Jungle Satyagrahis in Raipur jail — 39 people, calm, unbroken. Outside: the forest department officials signing the wage agreement and forced labour prohibition. The Satyagraha winning in jail what weapons could not win in the forest.

slides.text: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma arrived and explained that AIC approval had not been obtained for the full Satyagraha expansion. The movement was temporarily postponed. But the forest department had already conceded the minimum wages. The partial victory was permanent.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma arriving at the Jungle Satyagraha site — gently but firmly explaining the procedural requirement. The leaders accepting his counsel. The movement pausing. But the concession from the forest department already in writing. The win secured.

slides.text: February 5, 1922. Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement after the Chauri Chaura incident — where a crowd burned a police station, killing 22 officers. Gandhi could not accept violence. Chhattisgarh heard the withdrawal with discipline.
slides.visualDescription: The news of Chauri Chaura reaching Chhattisgarh — a burning police station in one frame, Gandhi's anguished face in another. The movement withdrawn. Chhattisgarh leaders receiving the news — disappointed but disciplined. The movement pausing, not ending.

slides.text: The Swaraj Party was formed in response to the withdrawal — Motilal Nehru and CR Das creating a mechanism for continued political pressure through the legislative councils. Chhattisgarh's leaders aligned with this new instrument of the freedom struggle.
slides.visualDescription: The Swaraj Party formation — a new political structure emerging from the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation. Chhattisgarh leaders in consultation about the new path. The movement adapting rather than stopping. Political creativity in the face of disappointment.

slides.text: The Jhanda Satyagraha of 1923. Pt. Sundarlal Sharma was arrested and sentenced to 6 months' imprisonment for hoisting the national flag in Jabalpur. The tricolor as an act of defiance — a piece of cloth that the British treated as a weapon.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma hoisting the tricolor flag at Jabalpur. British officers arresting him. The flag continuing to fly as he is led away. A flag as a Satyagraha. The cloth of three colors carrying the weight of a nation's aspiration. Six months in jail.

slides.text: Five leaders arrested in 1922 and imprisoned in Raipur Jail: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma, Narayan Rao Meghawale, Maulana Rauf, Maulana Hamid Ali, Bhagwati Prasad Mishra. Five men of different backgrounds sharing a cell and a cause.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur Jail — five men in one cell: Sharma, Meghawale, Maulana Rauf, Maulana Hamid Ali, Bhagwati Prasad Mishra. Hindu and Muslim leaders sharing imprisonment as they shared the movement. The jail cell as a microcosm of the unity they were fighting for.

slides.text: In jail, they remained unbroken. They read, they discussed, they planned. The British had imprisoned the leaders but could not imprison the movement. The Raipur DCC continued to function under other hands. The structure Shukla built proved its durability.
slides.visualDescription: Inside Raipur Jail — the five leaders in discussion, books and papers, planning continuing. Outside: the DCC under new leadership, still functioning. The movement proved to be larger than any individual. The organisation outlasting the imprisonment of its founders.

slides.text: March 12, 1930. Gandhi and 79 companions walked toward Dandi. Two hundred miles. Twenty-four days. April 6: Gandhi made salt on the seashore. The Salt March reached Chhattisgarh as electric news — and the province responded.
slides.visualDescription: The Salt March — Gandhi and companions walking through Gujarat. Then the news arriving in Chhattisgarh — people gathered around a radio, around a newspaper, faces transforming with the realisation of what is happening. The march reaching them through the air.

slides.text: In Dhamtari, Pt. Narayan Rao Meghawale made salt from soil using an ancient method. Karan C. Tejpal bought two grams of that salt for Rs 61. A symbolic act that cost a man's life savings for two grams of earth and water — and worth every rupee.
slides.visualDescription: Narayan Rao Meghawale at the edge of the Dhamtari pond, making salt from soil and water using ancient methods. Karan Tejpal paying Rs 61 for two grams. The transaction as ceremony, as defiance, as solidarity with Dandi from 700 kilometres away.

slides.text: Gandhi was arrested on May 5, 1930. Jungle Satyagrahas erupted across Chhattisgarh. The tribals entered the reserved forests again. The farmers refused the taxes again. The lawyers refused the courts again. The movement did not wait for Gandhi.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi arrested on May 5, 1930. Then across Chhattisgarh: Jungle Satyagrahis entering forests, farmers refusing tax collectors, lawyers closing offices. The movement continuing without its leader — proof that it had become genuinely the people's own.

slides.text: The Tamora Jungle Satyagraha of 1930 — seventeen days of sustained non-violent resistance in Mahasamund tehsil. Women standing before bayonets. Amar Singh shouting 'Mahatma Gandhi ki Jai' while being beaten. The land proving what it had learned.
slides.visualDescription: Tamora village, 1930 — tribal women standing in a line before British soldiers with bayonets, not moving. Amar Singh being beaten, still shouting Gandhi's name. Seventeen days of daily Satyagraha. The movement practiced with absolute discipline.

slides.text: In 1932, Congress was declared illegal. The leaders went underground or to jail. But the Raipur Congress Bhavan — constructed in 1940, inaugurated by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel — stood as proof that the organisation had not been killed by illegality.
slides.visualDescription: The Raipur Congress Bhavan — a building of purpose and permanence, constructed 1940. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel at the inauguration. The Congress declared illegal but building its house in Raipur. An institution that outlasted its suppression.

slides.text: The Raipur Conspiracy Case. Parasram Soni and BB Sur were charged with making explosives. Even as Gandhi preached non-violence, there were those in Chhattisgarh who chose harder paths. The freedom struggle contained multitudes.
slides.visualDescription: The Raipur Conspiracy Case — Parasram Soni and BB Sur in the British court on charges of making explosives. The harder edge of the freedom struggle that Gandhi's non-violence sought to channel. The movement containing both the charkha and the bomb.

slides.text: August 8, 1942. Gandhi's call: 'Karo ya Maro' — Do or Die. The Quit India Movement. Chhattisgarh's response was immediate. Leaders imprisoned, newspapers shut, public gatherings banned — and the movement continuing underground regardless.
slides.visualDescription: August 8, 1942 — the Quit India resolution. Karo ya Maro burning across Chhattisgarh. Leaders being rounded up. Newspapers shuttered. But in the back lanes and village squares, the movement continuing. The underground as the new front.

slides.text: Through it all — 1920 to 1947 — the leaders of Chhattisgarh held. Ravi Shankar Shukla. Pt. Sundarlal Sharma. Babu Chhotelal Srivastava. Thakur Pyarelal Singh. Ghanshyam Singh Gupta. E. Raghavendra Rao. Each paying their price and not stopping.
slides.visualDescription: A gallery of the six major leaders across 27 years — each face showing the marks of time, of imprisonment, of sustained commitment. Not diminished — deepened. The faces of people who chose something and stayed with the choice across decades.

slides.text: November 1933. Gandhi announces a nationwide Harijan tour to fight untouchability. After his agreement with Dr. Ambedkar — the Poona Pact — he has made a promise: to fight untouchability for the rest of his life. The tour starts from Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at Sevagram Ashram planning his Harijan tour — maps, itinerary, the Poona Pact on the table before him. The tour being announced. Then: the first pin placed on the map — Chhattisgarh. The second visit beginning to take shape thirteen years later.

slides.text: Between 1920 and 1933 — thirteen years. In those years, Chhattisgarh had Jungle Satyagrahas, a Salt March echo, civil disobedience, conspiracy cases, and the Quit India buildup. Not a quiet decade. A decade of sustained fire.
slides.visualDescription: Thirteen years compressed into a visual timeline: 1920, 1922, 1923, 1930, 1932, 1933. Each year a flame on the map of Chhattisgarh. The fire never going out between Gandhi's two visits. The province burning with its own purpose throughout.

slides.text: Gandhi had changed too. Between 1920 and 1933, he had led the Salt March, been imprisoned multiple times, signed the Poona Pact, made his promise to Ambedkar, and established Sevagram as his base. He was no longer Mohandas. He was The Mahatma.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's transformation between 1920 and 1933 — the younger, energetic Mohandas of the first visit becoming the aged, iconic Mahatma. The Salt March, imprisonment, Poona Pact shown in brief images. The man who returns will be different. The land will be the same.

slides.text: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma had continued his work on untouchability through all those years. By 1933, when Gandhi arrived, Sharma had been fighting this cause for nearly two decades. Gandhi would recognise this — and name him as his own guru.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma through the years — 1920, 1925, 1930, 1933 — each image showing him continuing his work on untouchability regardless of what else was happening in the movement. A man with one mission, pursued across decades without deviation.

slides.text: The women of Chhattisgarh had not stopped either. From the gold at Machilabad in 1920 to the bayonet line at Tamora in 1930 — ten years of women at the front of the movement, giving what they had, standing where they were needed.
slides.visualDescription: The women of Chhattisgarh's freedom movement from 1920 to 1933 — a visual sequence. Machilabad 1920: gold rings given. Tamora 1930: bayonet line held. Each image showing women not as supporters but as the core of the movement. Always there.

slides.text: The spark that Gandhi's first visit left in December 1920 — it stayed. It stayed through withdrawals and arrests and suppressions. It stayed in the homes where stage bricks sat on family altars. It stayed in Kandel, where the canal water flowed free.
slides.visualDescription: A Raipur family home — a brick from the Kankalipara stage on the family altar, a small lamp beside it. The canal at Kandel flowing. The charkha still turning. The spark made visible in small domestic sacred objects. History living in homes.

slides.text: Ravi Shankar Shukla — first secretary of the Raipur DCC in 1920 — would become the first Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh in 1947. The thread from December 1920 runs straight to August 15, 1947. One man, one city, one unbroken commitment.
slides.visualDescription: Ravi Shankar Shukla in 1920 — signing the DCC papers. Then Shukla in 1947 — hoisting the tricolor at Sitabardi Fort, Nagpur, as first CM of Madhya Pradesh. Twenty-seven years between the two images. The same man. The same commitment. The arc complete.

slides.text: Gandhi came to Chhattisgarh once as Mohandas. He was in the third-class compartment. He collected for the Tilak Fund. He went to a women's gathering. He stayed three days. And nothing was ever the same. Series 1 closes here.
slides.visualDescription: The closing image of Series 1 — Gandhi at the door of the third-class compartment, December 20, 1920, hands folded, the train moving. The simplest image. The most consequential. Three days that changed a province. Series 1: MOHANDAS — complete.

slides.text: November 1, 2000. The state of Chhattisgarh is formally established — separated from Madhya Pradesh after decades of campaigning. The land that Gandhi visited twice in 1920 and 1933 finally receives its own name, its own government, its own recognition.
slides.visualDescription: November 1, 2000 — the formation of Chhattisgarh state. The new state flag being raised. The map of India showing the new state boundary. The culmination of a struggle that Gandhi had touched in 1920 and 1933. The land named for itself at last.

slides.text: Johar — the Chhattisgarhi word of greeting and farewell. An expression of respect, of seeing, of meeting. To Gandhi, to his two visits, to the land that gave so much and asked so little: Johar.
slides.visualDescription: The word JOHAR in Devanagari script, large, golden, against the landscape of Chhattisgarh — its forests, its rivers, its ancient forts. The greeting and the farewell. Spoken now to the first series, to the first visit, to the men and women of this land.

slides.text: The words recorded on the pages of history may be blurred, but the words inscribed in the mind, heart, and memory of the people are indelible. Chhattisgarh gave strength and unconditional support to Mahatma Gandhi for the successful Indian freedom movement.
slides.visualDescription: History books with faded text — some pages blurred, some names missing. Then: the faces of ordinary people who remember. The elder who was there. The family who keeps the stage brick. The farmer whose grandfather won the Kandel Satyagraha. Living memory.

slides.text: Thirteen years will pass. He will return — not as Mohandas the lawyer and organiser, but as The Mahatma — the global icon returning to fight untouchability. The land will be different. The man will be different. The love will be the same.
slides.visualDescription: November 1933 — a train approaching Durg station. A different man inside than came in 1920. The elder Gandhi — iconic, global, transformed. Chhattisgarh in 1933 — also transformed by thirteen years of movement. Both changed. Both ready. The return.

slides.text: Series 1 — MOHANDAS — is complete. Ten episodes. The land of 36 forts. The first martyr. The earthquake of Bastar. The cannon at Jaistambh. The awakening. The water and the tax. The invitation. Mohandas arrives. The day in Dhamtari. The spark that stayed.
slides.visualDescription: The ten episode titles of Series 1 appearing one by one in their sequence — each with its defining image. A visual index of Series 1. The complete arc of MOHANDAS from 1825 to 1920. The foundation laid. Series 2 waiting.

slides.text: Thirteen years later, a changed man returns to a changed land. Series 2: THE MAHATMA — begins now.
slides.visualDescription: Bridge card between Series 1 and 2. Split image: Gandhi in 1920 (Mohandas) on the left, Gandhi in 1933 (The Mahatma) on the right. Thirteen years between them. The same man. Different weight. Different title. Series 2: THE MAHATMA — begins.
